title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
summary: Standard deep learning tools for regression and classification do not capture model uncertainty, while Bayesian models that do are computationally prohibitive. The paper proves that a neural network trained with dropout before every weight layer is mathematically equivalent to approximate variational inference in a deep Gaussian process, so predictive mean, variance and log-likelihood can be extracted from existing dropout models by averaging T stochastic forward passes ('MC dropout') without changing the model or optimisation. On the UCI regression benchmark of Hernández-Lobato & Adams (2015), dropout uncertainty outperforms variational inference (VI) and probabilistic back-propagation (PBP) in test RMSE and predictive log-likelihood on nearly all datasets, e.g. Boston Housing RMSE 2.97±0.19 vs 3.01±0.18 (PBP) and 4.32±0.29 (VI).

claims.statement: MC dropout achieves average test RMSE 2.97 on Boston Housing, beating PBP (3.01±0.18) and VI (4.32±0.29)
claims.table_ref: Table 1, row Boston Housing, column Dropout under 'Avg. Test RMSE and Std. Errors'
claims.config_for_value: Standard dropout NN replicating Hernández-Lobato & Adams (2015): 1 hidden layer of 50 units, dropout probabilities 0.05/0.005, dropout before every weight layer; prior length-scale l=10^-2; model precision τ found by Bayesian optimisation on validation log-likelihood using 40-iteration runs; final model trained with 10x more iterations (=400 epochs); minibatch size 32; Adam optimiser; weight decay λ set via τ = p l²/(2Nλ) (eq. 7); test RMSE from MC dropout, i.e. averaging T stochastic forward passes (eq. 6); average over 20 random splits
claims.reported_spread: ±0.19 (std. error over the 20 splits; October 2016 update corrected an earlier erroneously scaled-up value of 0.85)
claims.est_compute: CPU, ~1-2 hours total for all 20 splits including the τ search; each 400-epoch fit of the 50-unit net on ~455 training points takes seconds to a couple of minutes

match_target.why: Honours the user hint ('Table 1, Boston Housing, MC dropout test RMSE, 40-epoch x10 setting, 20 splits' = the Table 1 Dropout column trained with 10x the 40 BO epochs, i.e. 400 epochs). Boston is the smallest UCI dataset (N=506), the model is a single 50-unit hidden layer trained on CPU in seconds-to-minutes per split, and the value 2.97±0.19 is the headline of Table 1: dropout uncertainty matching/beating PBP (3.01) and clearly beating VI (4.32) - the paper's central quantitative result, not a side ablation.

tolerance.why: Rule 1: the paper reports a standard error for this exact value over the 20 random splits (±0.19); band = 3 x 0.19 = 0.57, kept at the two-decimal precision the paper prints.

requirements.stmt: Replicate the Hernández-Lobato & Adams (2015) regression set-up with a small standard dropout NN: a single hidden layer of 50 units (Table 2's caption confirms the Table 1 model has 1 layer: 'the same model again with 2 layers instead of 1')
requirements.quote: We used dropout with probabilities 0.05 and 0.005 since the network size is very small (with 50 units

requirements.stmt: Apply dropout before every weight layer of the network, sampling fresh Bernoulli masks per data point
requirements.quote: with dropout applied before every weight layer, is mathematically equivalent to an approximation

requirements.stmt: Use dropout probabilities 0.05 and 0.005 (small probabilities because the network is tiny)
requirements.quote: We used dropout with probabilities 0.05 and 0.005 since the network size is very small

requirements.stmt: Set the L2 weight decay λ from the model precision τ and prior length-scale l via the identity τ = p l²/(2Nλ) (eq. 7); τ and l only enter the training through this weight decay
Fix the prior length-scale l to 10^-2 for most datasets (Boston included by default)
requirements.quote: set the prior length-scale to 10−2 for most datasets based on the range of the data

requirements.stmt: Find the model precision τ per dataset/split by Bayesian optimisation over validation log-likelihood (Spearmint-style BO), as in Hernández-Lobato & Adams (2015)
requirements.quote: we use Bayesian optimisation (BO, (Snoek et al., 2012; Snoek & authors, 2015)) over validation log-likelihood to find optimal τ

requirements.stmt: Run BO candidates for 40 iterations/epochs, then train the final model with 10x more iterations (=400 epochs); this is the Table 1 '40-epoch x10' setting (Table 2's '10x Epochs', 4000 epochs, is a different, later setting)
requirements.quote: The BO runs used 40 iterations following the original setup, but after finding the optimal parameter values we used 10x more iterations

requirements.stmt: Optimise with Adam and mini-batches of size 32
requirements.quote: Finally, we used mini-batches of size 32 and the Adam optimiser (Kingma & Ba, 2014).

requirements.stmt: Compute predictions by MC dropout (eq. 6): at test time keep dropout active, perform T stochastic forward passes and average the outputs to get the predictive mean
requirements.quote: In practice this is equivalent to performing T stochastic forward passes through the network and averaging the results.

requirements.stmt: The Table 1 dropout RMSE must come from this MC average, not from standard weight averaging (multiplying weights by p at test time)
requirements.quote: Dropout's RMSE in table 1 is given by averaging stochastic forward passes through the network following eq. (6)

requirements.stmt: Evaluate on 20 random splits of the data and report the average test metric with its standard error (Boston, like most datasets, uses 20 splits; only Protein uses 5 and Year 1)
requirements.quote: All experiments were averaged on 20 random splits of the data

requirements.stmt: Follow the datasets, protocol and metric definitions of Hernández-Lobato & Adams (2015) so the numbers are comparable to VI and PBP
requirements.quote: We replicate the experiment set-up in Hern ́andez-Lobato & Adams (2015) and compare the RMSE and predictive log-likelihood

requirements.stmt: For the log-likelihood claims, estimate predictive log-likelihood by Monte Carlo integration (eq. 8: logsumexp over T stochastic passes of -||y-ŷt||²/(2τ), minus log T and Gaussian normalisers) using the tuned τ
requirements.quote: We can estimate our predictive log-likelihood by Monte Carlo integration of eq. (2).

data.name: Boston Housing (UCI)
data.how_to_get: UCI Machine Learning Repository: https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/machine-learning-databases/housing/housing.data (506 rows, 13 features). The exact 20 random splits used by the paper are bundled in the authors' code repo https://github.com/yaringal/DropoutUncertaintyExps (UCI data folder).

data.name: UCI regression suite (Concrete Strength, Energy Efficiency, Kin8nm, Naval Propulsion, Power Plant, Protein Structure, Wine Quality Red, Yacht Hydrodynamics, Year Prediction MSD)
data.how_to_get: All available from the UCI Machine Learning Repository; pre-processed copies with the Hernández-Lobato & Adams split files ship with https://github.com/yaringal/DropoutUncertaintyExps and the PBP authors' code.

data.name: Mauna Loa CO2 concentrations (qualitative extrapolation experiment)
data.how_to_get: Scripps/NOAA Mauna Loa in-situ monthly mean CO2 (Keeling et al., 2004); the paper uses a ~200-point centred and normalised subset.

data.name: MNIST (classification uncertainty experiment)
data.how_to_get: http://yann.lecun.com/exdb/mnist/ or the copy bundled with any deep-learning framework.

stated_compute: No hardware is stated. The paper reports wall-clock times only: 'On Naval Propulsion for example our model takes 276 seconds on average per split (start-to-finish, divided by the number of splits).' and 'For Kin8nm our model requires 188 seconds on average including BO, 65 seconds without, compared to PBP's 156 seconds.' Software: Keras on Theano for the regression experiments, Caffe for the MNIST LeNet experiment, Spearmint for Bayesian optimisation, convnetjs for the RL experiment.
